title: Grandmaster Naroditsky | Chess Speedrun | 2140
openingName: King's Indian Defense (vs the Torre Attack)

moves.spoken: White plays the Torre Attack — the bishop to g5, the same spirit as the London but with the bishop on g5 instead of f4.
White develops the bishop to c4, a slightly unusual choice — normally it goes to d3 or e2 in the Torre.
We keep the King's-Indian character with d6, not d5 — d5 would drift into Grünfeld territory. The beauty of the KID is you barely change your moves for what White does.
The KID has two pawn breaks — c5 and e5 — and the whole point of the Torre's bishop on g5 is to discourage e5 with a nasty pin. So we don't rush into it; we finish developing first.
teaches: the c5 and e5 breaks; beware the pin on e5

moves.spoken: We fianchetto the light-squared bishop to b7 rather than g4 — a bishop developed to g4 has no retreat, and h3 would simply trap it.
teaches: fianchetto to keep the bishop safe

moves.spoken: The bishop settles on b7, raking down the long diagonal.
We meet White's queenside expansion with a5 of our own, freezing his a-pawn.
teaches: a5 to stop the a4-a5 push

moves.spoken: The knight develops to d7, not c6, so it doesn't block our fianchetto bishop. From here the plan is clear: break the pin with g5 and h5 when needed, pile pieces onto the kingside — the queen to f6 and beyond — and eventually launch the e5 and f5-f4 pawn storm, opening the h-file at White's king and overloading the f3-knight.
teaches: Nd7 keeps the bishop’s diagonal open
accumulate on the kingside, then storm
plans: open the h-file, overload the f3-knight

moves.spoken: The Torre Attack is named for Carlos Torre of Mexico — though the modern move order owes as much to Eugenio Torre of the Philippines, who played it dozens of times decades later. A nice piece of trivia behind a very practical opening.
